motivo: Reportaje de reserva, sin mensajes de la semana. El jefe de reportajes eligió el coste ambiental de la IA: ningún reportaje lo ha tratado, sale en ChatGPT-IA-edu desde 2024 con debate de argumentos (y como objeción en los centros), tiene actores con documentos propios (AIE, Google, OpenAI, Mistral, ONU, UE) y marco en España, y las dos fichas de la Biblioteca que lo tocan (la guía 2.0 del INTEF y el manual del CESDi) repiten de segunda mano cifras que no verifican. No depende de la fecha: todas las cifras van fechadas.
titular: AI uses energy and water, but the per-query figures in circulation measure different things
entradilla: The data centres that run artificial intelligence consume more electricity every year, as the International Energy Agency estimates, and water too. The “per question” figures repeated in guides and staff rooms, however, come from calculations made in 2023 and change depending on what is measured and who measures it. This report explains where each number comes from, what European law requires companies to disclose and how to turn that uncertainty into a classroom activity.

apartados.ladillo: The figures in the guides come from calculations made in 2023
parrafos: In ChatGPT-IA-edu the environmental impact of AI has been coming up for years. In October 2025, a teacher said that at their school AI was rejected with two arguments: that there were already teachers and that it [“uses a lot of water”](https://t.me/ChatGPTedu/41255). In September 2026 a trainer’s idea was picked up: the debate swings between celebrating AI uncritically and rejecting it with [arguments based on fear, without going into detail](https://t.me/ChatGPTedu/52604). As early as October 2024 the group discussed whether the cost lies only in developing the models or also in [everyone’s use of them](https://t.me/ChatGPTedu/16193), whether it is enough to [compare cost and benefit](https://t.me/ChatGPTedu/16195) and why [social media or mobile phones](https://t.me/ChatGPTedu/16205) are not looked at in the same way.

Educational guides have put two specific figures on paper. The [INTEF guide 2.0 on AI in education, which this paper covered](pieza:2026-11-16/intef-guia-ia-v2), states that a query to a generative AI consumes ten times more electricity than a traditional search and that between ten and fifty questions are equivalent to half a litre of water. The urgent manual from the CESDi at the National University of General San Martín repeats the first figure, based on a 2024 report from Tecnológico de Monterrey. The same comparison circulated in the group in [an article shared in October 2024](https://t.me/ChatGPTedu/16410).

The electricity figure has a traceable origin. According to an analysis by Josh You for [Epoch AI](https://epoch.ai/gradient-updates/how-much-energy-does-chatgpt-use), an AI research centre, the estimate of about 3 watt-hours (Wh) per query comes from a 2023 calculation by Alex de Vries, which in turn was based on an estimate from February 2023 for GPT-3.5: chips from an earlier generation and answers of 2,000 *tokens* (word fragments), which the author considers unrepresentative. Epoch AI redid the sum in February 2025 for GPT-4o and arrived at about 0.3 Wh per typical query, ten times less, and still considers it a pessimistic estimate.

The water figure comes from the study [“Making AI Less ‘Thirsty’”](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03271), by Pengfei Li, Jianyi Yang, Mohammad A. Islam and Shaolei Ren, whose first version dates from April 2023. It calculates that GPT-3 needed half a litre of water for roughly 10 to 50 medium-length responses, depending on when and where it was run. **That sum adds the water that evaporates in cooling the data centre and the water consumed by the power stations that produce its electricity**, which accounts for most of it: in the US average given by the study, 14.7 of the 16.9 millilitres per response.

apartados.ladillo: Google, OpenAI and Mistral measure different queries
parrafos: In the summer of 2025, three companies published figures of their own. On 21 August 2025 Google released [a blog post](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/infrastructure/measuring-the-environmental-impact-of-ai-inference) and [a technical paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15734) signed by company staff: the median text query to the Gemini app, with data from May 2025, uses 0.24 Wh, emits 0.03 grams of CO₂ equivalent and consumes 0.26 millilitres of water, about five drops. Its method also counts idle machines and cooling. Google itself warns that nobody outside the company has verified the data.

OpenAI’s figure does not come from a study but from a post on the blog of its chief executive, Sam Altman, [“The Gentle Singularity”](https://blog.samaltman.com/the-gentle-singularity), from June 2025: the average ChatGPT query uses about 0.34 Wh and 0.000085 gallons of water, about 0.3 millilitres, with no explanation of the method or the model. On 22 July 2025 Mistral AI published [a life-cycle analysis](https://mistral.ai/news/our-contribution-to-a-global-environmental-standard-for-ai), carried out with the consultancy Carbone 4 and the French agency ADEME, which includes the manufacture of the servers. According to the company, a 400-*token* response from its assistant Le Chat accounts for 1.14 grams of CO₂ equivalent and 45 millilitres of water.

Sasha Luccioni and Theo Alves Da Costa, of the company Hugging Face, compared the three disclosures on 17 September 2025 in [an analysis on its blog](https://huggingface.co/blog/sasha/environmental-impact-disclosures): each company uses different methods and assumptions. Google counts only the water used in its own data centres, not that of the power stations; OpenAI does not say what an average query is or which model it measures; Mistral does not give the electricity per response. The size of the query also changes the result: Epoch AI estimates that with a long document it can be around 2.5 Wh.

tabla.nota: The figures are not comparable with one another: the model, the year, the mean or median, the size of the query and the share of the cost that is counted all differ. The companies’ figures are the companies’ own.

apartados.ladillo: The total cost grows even if each query costs less
parrafos: According to the International Energy Agency (IEA) report [“Energy and AI”](https://www.iea.org/reports/energy-and-ai/executive-summary), from 2025, data centres consumed about 415 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2024, around 1.5% of the world’s electricity, and will reach about 945 TWh in 2030, slightly more than Japan consumes today. In its April 2026 update, [“Key Questions on Energy and AI”](https://www.iea.org/reports/key-questions-on-energy-and-ai/executive-summary), the IEA estimates that consumption rose by 17% in 2025, to 485 TWh, and that that of AI-focused centres grew by 50%. At the same time, **the energy used by each AI task has fallen by at least a factor of ten per year** in recent years, according to the same agency.

Google illustrates both trends at once. According to its technical paper, the energy of its median query fell by a factor of 33 between May 2024 and May 2025, and its emissions by a factor of 44. But in [its environmental report of 30 June 2026](https://blog.google/company-news/outreach-and-initiatives/sustainability/2026-environmental-report/), the company reports for 2025 a 37% rise in its electricity demand, the largest in its history, and 25% more emissions in its supply chain. Luccioni and Alves Da Costa sum it up this way: the cost per unit can fall while the units multiply and the total grows.

Which phase uses most also matters. According to the press release from United Nations University (UNU) on the report [“Environmental Cost of AI’s Energy Use: Carbon, Water and Land Footprints”](https://unu.edu/inweh/news/environmental-cost-of-AIs-Enrgy-Use-carbon-water-and-land-footprints), from its water institute (UNU-INWEH) and dated 3 June 2026, using already trained models accounts for between 80% and 90% of AI’s energy; training them is the rest. The release also warns that emitting little carbon does not mean using little water: with different electricity or in an area with less water, the same response leaves a different footprint. A [press report on a UN study](https://t.me/ChatGPTedu/49276) on this subject was shared in the group on 4 June.

apartados.ladillo: The EU asks for energy data that the public does not see
parrafos: [Regulation (EU) 2024/1689](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng), the European AI Act, has required since 2 August 2025 companies offering general-purpose models, such as those behind ChatGPT or Gemini, to document “the known or estimated energy consumption of the model” (Annex XI); if they do not know it, they may estimate it from the computing resources used. According to Article 53, that documentation is for the European AI Office and national authorities when they ask for it, not for the public. For a school, the regulation adds no obligation on this point, and as of November 2026 there is no public label showing the consumption of each tool.

Data centres have rules of their own. The European energy efficiency directive and [Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2024/1364/oj/eng) require those with an IT power demand of 500 kilowatts or more to publish energy and sustainability indicators every year and to submit them, before 15 May, to a European database, as the [Spanish Ministry for the Ecological Transition](https://www.miteco.gob.es/es/energia/eficiencia/centros-de-datos.html) (in Spanish) explains. The ministry is also processing a royal decree on sustainability for these centres, with public hearings in 2025 and 2026; as of November 2026, its page does not show it as approved.

In schools, the subject already has a place. [Royal Decree 217/2022](https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2022-4975), setting the minimum curriculum for compulsory secondary education (ESO, ages 12 to 16), includes in digital competence (descriptor CD4) that students should also protect the environment when using technology and make critical and sustainable use of it. Among the ten ethical principles of the INTEF guide is that of well-being and sustainability. And in EduMedia-IAG, members [shared the priorities of the computer science teachers’ association CSTA and of AI4K12](https://t.me/EduMediaIAG/1148), which in their [2025 proposal](https://csteachers.org/ai-priorities/) call for exploring the environmental impact of AI in grades 3 to 5, investigating its positive and negative effects in grades 6 to 8 and designing ways to reduce them in grades 9 to 12.

apartados.ladillo: Tracing a figure works as an activity in any subject
parrafos: A teacher does not have to choose between “AI uses a lot of water” and “it is a drop in the ocean”: they can turn the question into an activity at no cost for science, technology, geography or Civic and Ethical Values Education. Step one: bring to class a figure from a guide, a news item or a message and trace its origin, with three questions: what year is it from, which model was measured and what share of the cost was counted. With the table in this report it becomes clear that the half litre and the five drops do not contradict each other: they measure different things.

Step two: compare orders of magnitude with everyday uses and ask who is making the comparison. Google equates its median query to about nine seconds of television and Altman to what an oven uses in a little over a second: both comparisons come from the companies. To try out scenarios, [What Uses More?](https://what-uses-more.com/) is useful, an online tool created by Jon Ippolito in the Learn with AI initiative and [shared in the group in September 2025](https://t.me/ChatGPTedu/38136): it compares the energy and water of AI tasks with a search or a film, and warns that its values are estimates based on incomplete and often contradictory sources.

Step three: agree criteria for use with students. According to [the report by UNESCO and University College London (UCL)](https://www.unesco.org/es/articles/modelos-de-lenguaje-grandes-de-ia-un-nuevo-informe-revela-como-reducir-el-consumo-de-energia-en-un) (in Spanish) from July 2025, small models adapted to a task can cut consumption “by up to 90%”, and shorter prompts and responses “by more than 50%”, in the study’s experiments. **Using the lightest model that does the job is the shared recommendation of UNU and UNESCO**, and the study “[Power Hungry Processing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.16863)”, by Luccioni, Yacine Jernite and Emma Strubell (2023), found that general-purpose generative models use orders of magnitude more than single-task ones. In practice: a search engine or a dictionary for a fact, specific requests and no generating images by trial and error.

None of these sources asks for AI to be given up: the IEA expects data-centre consumption to double by 2030 even if each task becomes more efficient, and one of the authors of the UNU report makes clear that it is not a case against artificial intelligence.

claves: Data centres are consuming more and more electricity: the IEA estimates 485 TWh in 2025 and close to 950 TWh in 2030.
The per-query figures in the guides (“ten times a search”, “half a litre per 10 to 50 questions”) are 2023 estimates for the models of that time.
Google, OpenAI and Mistral published figures of their own in 2025 that are not comparable: each measures a different query and counts different parts of the cost.
The European AI Act requires the energy consumption of models to be documented, but for the authorities, not for the public.
In class, tracing the origin of a figure and choosing the lightest model that does the job are two activities that cost nothing.

Grupos, con la página de cada mensaje: 41255, 52604, 16193, 16195, 16205, 16410, 38136 y 49276 dicen lo que el texto les atribuye; de 49276 solo se confirma una noticia del diari ARA sobre un informe de la ONU, no que sea el de la UNU, y así se dice. Los mensajes de EduMedia-IAG 1148-1153 son de un autor del diario que cita el informe de la CSTA; se enlaza el 1148, que trae el enlace, y no se nombra a nadie. Ninguna persona que opina está nombrada; Jon Ippolito es el autor del recurso. No se pudo comprobar: el PDF de la guía del INTEF (las cifras de diez veces y medio litro se toman de la ficha publicada por el diario el 16-11-2026, y las del manual del CESDi de la del 21-11-2026) ni el texto de Joule de De Vries (403) ni el anexo del Reglamento Delegado 2024/1364 (EUR-Lex vacío; el título sale de la búsqueda). Quitado o suavizado por no confirmarse: la fecha del día de Altman; que el Joule sea de octubre de 2023; que las cifras del INTEF vengan de sus referencias y no se comprueben; «gratuita» de What Uses More; que OpenAI «no ha publicado un estudio» (ahora, que la cifra viene de una entrada de blog); el crecimiento del agua en el titular. El enlace pieza:2026-11-21/manual-ia-aula-abya-yala se quita porque su clave no está en publicado.txt. Los fragmentos recortados para ajustar la extensión (Mistral Large 2, 100.000 tokens, imágenes y vídeo, 200 y 1.450 veces, agua devuelta por Google, tabla de Washington e Irlanda) estaban confirmados.
ilustracion: Infografía en dos mitades. A la izquierda, «Cada consulta»: una fila de seis vasos de agua de tamaños muy distintos, rotulados con su fuente y año (Li 2023, Mistral 2025, Altman 2025, Google 2025), con una lupa que muestra qué cuenta cada uno (solo el centro de datos, también la central eléctrica, también la fabricación). A la derecha, «Todos los centros de datos»: columnas de electricidad de la AIE que crecen de 415 TWh en 2024 a 485 TWh en 2025 y unos 950 TWh en 2030.
